questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{3x+1}$ and the point $P(21,4)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(21,4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt[3]{3x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{(3x+1)^{2/3}} \\ {f}^{′}(21) & =\frac{1}{(64)^{2/3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(21,4)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(4,21)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$ 

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(21)} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we have

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(1)=2$ and ${f}^{′}(2)=-7.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-7)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(4).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(4)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(4) & =x \\ f(x) & =4 \\ {5}^{x}+3 & =4 \\ {5}^{x} & =1 \\ {5}^{x} & ={5}^{0} \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(4)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={5}^{x}+3 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={5}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & ={5}^{0}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ (x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=2.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)+\frac{x+3}{x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+\frac{2+3}{2-1} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =0+5 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
